description: Coordinate three independently running workers so their work completes in role order 0, 1, 2, regardless of thread launch or scheduling order. Implement RunOrdered(role,context), called once by each worker with its role. Call that worker context.Work() exactly once. Work for role 1 must not begin until role 0 work finishes; role 2 must wait for role 1 work to finish. Returning or sorting a list does not perform the work.
constraints: The judge starts three real threads (Node worker_threads for JavaScript), each calling the same implementation independently with role 0, 1 or 2. Each worker receives its own wrapper around one shared SyncContext state. Use only the provided context API for coordination and work. Return void/None/undefined. Do not launch extra threads or use sleeps, delays or polling as a substitute for synchronization.

context.Wait(gate) atomically consumes a permit from gate 0 or 1, blocking until one exists. context.Signal(gate) adds one permit and wakes a waiter. Both counting-semaphore gates start with zero permits and belong to this one case. Calls on an invalid gate, more than 20 total Wait/Signal/Work calls per worker or a context from another worker fail the case. Wait/Signal are thread-safe; caller work is not automatically ordered.

context.Work() invokes opaque actual work owned by that worker; it may take time before returning. It must execute exactly once in each worker, and no dependent worker may begin its Work until its predecessor Work returns. Primitive calls may synchronize the workers but must not run another role work on their behalf. Contexts are opaque supplied objects; their fields/underlying shared storage must not be inspected or altered.

JSON launchOrder is a permutation of [0,1,2]; delayMask is a test scheduling input in 0..3; the context wire placeholder is []. These are private judge inputs, not the callable parameters: the callable receives role and its provided context. The judge varies launch order and independent entry delays without revealing a required sleep duration. A bounded execution timeout rejects noncompletion; passing sampled schedules alone is not a proof for every scheduler.

The displayed result is a private completion-order observation [0,1,2], never a return value to construct. Instances have independent gates and work state. No fairness bound or real-time latency guarantee is required; assume runnable threads are eventually scheduled.
why: Create one synchronization edge after each predecessor finishes its Work. Role 0 signals gate 0 only after returning from Work; role 1 must consume that permit before entering Work, then signals gate 1 afterward. Role 2 consumes gate 1 before entering Work. Semaphore permits persist when a signal happens before the corresponding wait, so neither launch order nor a guessed delay matters.
correctness: Gate 0 initially has no permit and only role 0 signals it, after its Work returns. Therefore role 1 cannot pass its Wait until role 0 completes. Similarly gate 1 is signaled only after role 1 Work returns, so role 2 starts only after role 1 completes. Each worker calls Work exactly once and each required signal/wait occurs once. There is no wait in role 0, so it eventually finishes and enables role 1, which eventually enables role 2 under eventual scheduling. Signals before waits remain available and do not create lost wakeups. Both required completion dependencies and termination follow without relying on timing.
walkthrough: Suppose workers start in order [2,1,0]. Role 2 blocks on gate 1; role 1 blocks on gate 0. Role 0 performs its Work and then signals gate 0. Role 1 consumes that permit, performs its Work and signals gate 1. Role 2 now performs its Work. If role 0 instead finishes before role 1 starts, gate 0 retains its permit and the same order follows.
time: O(1) synchronization operations per worker and O(W0+W1+W2) required sequential work duration, excluding unbounded scheduler waiting; no spin loop is used.
space: O(1) shared semaphore state and O(1) local storage per worker, excluding the judge worker stacks and opaque work.
edges: All six thread launch orders, signals before waits and predecessor entry delays.
Work completion rather than only start order; guessed sleeps are insufficient.
Repeated independent cases must not reuse stale permits or static work state.
Missing work, duplicate work, wrong gate and deadlock must fail.
related: The public Foo implementation establishes first/second/third work ordering through two semaphores. This callable supplies those two initially empty gates and private work callbacks so the grader can execute native workers and observe completion dependencies in every supported language.

languageWhy.csharp: C# RunOrdered uses the supplied SyncContext semaphore operations synchronously from real managed Thread instances. The Signal call follows Work return, rather than merely the beginning of work.
languageWhy.java: Java calls the supplied context from three real Thread instances. Semaphore acquisition supplies the dependency before Work and release follows completion; no Thread.sleep assumption appears in the submitted method.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ receives SyncContext by reference, borrowing judge-owned shared coordination state. Wait/Signal block and signal native condition-variable semaphore permits; the method owns no thread or context lifetime.
languageWhy.python: Python uses the supplied blocking semaphore API from threading.Thread workers. The GIL does not replace the two ordering edges, particularly while Work or Wait blocks; explicit waits/signals establish completion dependencies.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript runs the same synchronous function in three Node worker_threads. Provided Wait/Signal use shared-memory Atomics coordination across isolates, rather than Promise callbacks on one event loop. The function never sorts or returns completion events.

description: Coordinate four independently running FizzBuzz workers to print exactly the values for 1 through limit, in increasing numeric order. Role 0 prints ordinary numbers, role 1 prints Fizz for multiples of 3 only, role 2 prints Buzz for multiples of 5 only, and role 3 prints FizzBuzz for multiples of both. Implement RunFizzBuzz(role,limit,context), called once by each actual worker. Use context.Print(value) for that worker assigned items; do not return an output array or run every role from one worker.
constraints: limit is 0..100. Four real native threads (Node worker_threads in JavaScript) call the implementation with distinct roles 0..3, sharing a supplied FizzContext coordination state. Each call returns void/None/undefined. The judge chooses launch order and independent entry delays. Assume eventually scheduled runnable workers, not a particular order or maximum scheduling latency.

context.Wait(gate) consumes one counting-semaphore permit from gate 0..3, blocking if empty; Signal(gate) adds one permit. Initially only gate 0 has one permit, all other gates have zero. Gates belong to this case, never previous cases. Use only these supplied primitives and Print for coordination; no extra threads, sleeps or polling. Each worker may make at most 4*(limit+1) total API calls; invalid gates and foreign-worker contexts fail.

context.Print(value) performs the current worker actual output work and may take time before returning. It accepts only the next integer in 1..limit and only from the assigned role: both-divisible first, then only-3, only-5 or ordinary-number role. Calls must not overlap or duplicate an item. It emits the corresponding Fizz/Buzz/FizzBuzz token or invariant decimal number; its output is observed privately, not built by your return value.

A JSON fixture contains limit, a permutation launchOrder of [0,1,2,3], scheduling delayMask in 0..15, and [] for the context. These are private scheduling inputs; the callable receives role, limit and an opaque context, not a launch-order array. Do not inspect context internals or underlying shared memory. Contexts and permits are isolated across cases.

Displayed output is the private printed-token transcript. For limit=0, no worker prints and all four return. Every value 1..limit must be printed exactly once in order, including limit when it is divisible by 3, 5 or both. A bounded runtime timeout rejects noncompletion; sampled schedules supplement the synchronization proof, not a universal scheduler guarantee.
why: The roles can determine their own values from divisibility; only the order between roles needs coordination. Keep one permit as a baton for the next value. A worker waits on its role gate before printing its value, then signals the role responsible for the next integer after printing finishes. Consecutive ordinary numbers can pass the baton back to the same gate, whose permit persists until the next wait.
correctness: Initially value 1 belongs to ordinary role 0, which alone has a permit. Assume exactly values 1 through v-1 have completed and the sole permit belongs to the role for v. Other roles wait without printing. The owner eventually consumes its permit, prints v from its own worker, and only after Print returns signals the owner of v+1 when one exists. This preserves increasing, nonoverlapping, exactly-once output and the baton invariant. Each role scans values increasingly, so it reaches each of its required waits in order and cannot skip an owned item. The final value needs no successor signal, and all remaining role iterations perform no work; all workers return. For limit=0 all loops are empty. Both-divisible ownership is tested first, preventing duplicate Fizz/Buzz output at multiples of 15.
walkthrough: For limit 5, role 0 consumes its initial permit and prints 1, then signals gate 0 for 2. After printing 2 it signals gate 1, so the Fizz worker prints value 3 as Fizz. That worker signals gate 0 for 4; after 4, role 0 signals gate 2 so Buzz prints value 5. No successor signal is needed. The private transcript is ["1","2","Fizz","4","Buzz"], regardless of worker launch order.
time: O(limit) total scanning work across four fixed workers and O(limit) synchronization/output calls. Required output work is sequential by specification; elapsed time also includes unbounded scheduler waiting, so no real-time bound is claimed.
space: O(1) algorithmic shared gate state and scalar local state per worker, excluding judge-owned thread stacks, print callback and observed output transcript.
edges: limit 0/1 and endpoints divisible by 3, 5 or both.
All 24 launch orders, delayed owning worker and consecutive ordinary values.
Wrong printing role, duplicate/omitted output and overlapping calls are invalid.
Independent repeated cases must not inherit permits or static counters.
related: The primary QuestionB/FizzBuzzThread/NumberThread variant runs four real workers. QuestionA sequential FizzBuzz is not substituted. This independent solution uses explicit counting-permit handoffs instead of the public busy-polling shared-counter implementation.
